choices: One original strand and one new strand

checkpoints.prompt: Must a cell replicate (copy) its DNA each time it wants to transcribe an mRNA message?
checkpoints.context: Replication makes a new copy of DNA. Transcription uses a gene’s DNA instructions to make messenger RNA (mRNA).
choices: Yes. It must copy the DNA before making each mRNA message.
No. It can transcribe the same gene many times using the DNA already in the nucleus.

limits: This virtual model follows one gene in a cell with a nucleus. Shapes, colors, sizes, and speeds help show the steps. They are not to scale. The DNA and RNA sections are much shorter than real genes. The promoter and intron are markers, not full sequences. RNA parts outside the code are shortened or left out. Primers and many helper proteins are provided. Tail-cutting helpers are also provided. Opening DNA and copying it can happen together in cells. RNA processing can begin while RNA is still being made. At each fork, the leading strand is copied continuously. The lagging strand is copied in short pieces called Okazaki fragments. Primase starts each piece with an RNA primer. DNA polymerase adds DNA. Other enzymes replace the RNA primers with DNA. DNA ligase seals the joins. These extra steps are not shown in this model. The first tRNA starts in the ribosome’s P site. Later tRNAs enter its A site. The model provides the helpers for these steps. The three amino acids make a short peptide, not a full working protein. This model does not show bacteria, mitochondria, or chloroplasts.
